episode_title: AI Still Needs Your Judgment, with Doug Gabbard | Episode #0037

real_qa.q: How can ChatGPT help photographers and creative professionals learn Adobe Photoshop and Lightroom without memorizing complex terminology?
real_qa.r: You can take a screenshot of the dialog box or menu you're stuck in, paste it into ChatGPT, and describe what you're trying to achieve. ChatGPT will provide detailed guidance without requiring you to know all the terminology. Doug uses this method when trying to create automated actions in Photoshop—he can show the interface and ask what he's trying to do, and it responds with helpful details about whether he's in the right place or needs to navigate elsewhere.

real_qa.q: What is the Azure Archive Storage service level agreement for data retrieval and what is the cost difference compared to hot storage for large photo backups?
real_qa.r: Azure Archive Storage has an SLA of three to five days for retrieval because the data is not online—once files are placed in archive, they go offline. Doug pays less than $10 per month for 14 terabytes in Azure Archive Storage, and retrieval costs approximately $150 if needed. This contrasts sharply with hot storage options like Backblaze, which would cost over $100 per month for the same 14 terabytes.
real_qa.requete: Azure Archive Storage SLA retrieval time cost

real_qa.q: How does AI need human judgment when generating code or automation scripts for infrastructure, particularly regarding scalability and security?
real_qa.r: AI will generate code that works for a single use case but may fail at scale or in production environments if you don't specifically ask for security measures, error checking, and scalability considerations. For example, code written for one server looks very different from code designed for 2,000 or 5,000 servers. You must remember to request error checking, handle bad input validation (letters versus numbers), and consider whether the solution needs to work on-premises, in the cloud, or internationally—aspects that professionals learned through experience but must now explicitly instruct AI to address.
real_qa.requete: AI code scalability security error checking infrastructure

real_qa.q: What was Doug Gabbard's experience with SimpliSafe's customer support chatbot and how did it demonstrate early AI limitations in technical troubleshooting?
real_qa.r: About three years ago, when Doug's SimpliSafe base station stopped working, he chatted with their bot which correctly diagnosed low batteries but then suggested wiping corroded batteries and reinserting them—advice that wouldn't solve the actual problem. Although the bot interaction felt natural and personal, it demonstrated that early AI-driven support could provide plausible but technically incorrect solutions, though Doug noted the bot was ahead of its time for deploying conversational AI in customer support.
real_qa.requete: SimpliSafe chatbot AI customer support experience

real_qa.q: Why do AI language models sometimes provide incorrect answers even on well-established technical topics, and how should professionals validate AI-generated information?
real_qa.r: When Doug asked ChatGPT an Active Directory question he knew extremely well, it gave a blatantly wrong answer. When he corrected it, the AI explained that it had provided the more prevalent answer it found in its training data rather than the correct technical answer. This illustrates that you cannot rely entirely on AI—you must have foundational knowledge to recognize when it's telling you something wrong. If you're totally ignorant on a subject, you should be careful because the AI will confidently give advice that may not be right.
real_qa.requete: ChatGPT wrong answer why Active Directory validation

He is deeply knowledgeable in infrastructure, cloud architecture, and Active Directory, and applies his professional expertise to creative workflows involving photography, drone videography, and real estate photography.
